RESULT — full two-stage analysis executed (script: analysis.py, full output saved to analysis_output.txt).

**HYPOTHESIS (answering "How does the consideration of academic characteristics alter the effects of SES and race on BA degree completion?"):**
Considering academic characteristics substantially *attenuates* the effect of race on BA-level attainment: the Black disadvantage shrinks by **~65%** (−0.82 → −0.29 grade-years, still significant at p<10⁻⁵) and the Hispanic disadvantage is **fully absorbed and reverses sign** (−0.42 → +0.24), indicating that academic ability (ASVAB, 1981) mediates most of the racial gap in attainment. The SES effect, measured by parent education, is also attenuated by **~57%** (0.158 → 0.069 per parent grade-year) once ability is controlled. By contrast, 1978 family income — which is not a positive predictor of attainment in the first place (b=−0.007, ns) — shows a *suppression* effect: its coefficient becomes negative and significant (−0.131, p<10⁻⁹) after adding ASVAB, because income is weakly related to grades (r=0.015) but strongly to ability (r=0.241). The academic characteristic itself is the single strongest predictor (ASVAB composite: 1 SD ≈ 0.78–0.86 grade-years; standardized β=0.35). In short: adding academic characteristics removes roughly two-thirds of the Black attainment gap, eliminates (and reverses) the Hispanic gap, and cuts the parent-education SES effect by more than half; residual race/SES effects are small relative to ability.

**Sample (complete cases) & race composition:** Stage A (income): n=10,073 (Black 16.2% / Hispanic 24.9% / White 58.9%); Stage B (+ASVAB): n=8,928 (16.5/25.9/57.6); Stage B2 (+class-rank pct): n=4,174 (13.8/23.0/63.2); parent-ed A/B: n=12,099/10,675; wealth A/B: n=8,795/8,083; logit college A/B: n=10,195/9,036.

**Primary OLS (outcome = Highest grade completed, 1979; BA = 16):**
| Coef | Stage A (race+income) | Stage B (+ASVAB) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Black | −0.821 (p<1e-35) | −0.287 (p=9e-6) | **−65.0% attenuated** |
| Hispanic | −0.422 (p<1e-13) | +0.240 (p=3e-5) | **fully attenuated, sign reversal** |
| Income(log) | −0.007 (ns) | −0.131 (p<1e-9) | suppression (not attenuation) |
| ASVAB_z | — | +0.779 (p<1e-190) | β_std=0.35 |
Sex-adjusted versions nearly identical (Black 64.7% attenuation; Hispanic reversal).

**Sensitivity analyses:**
- Parent-education composite: Black −0.289→−0.129 (**55% attenuation**), Hispanic −0.195→+0.276 (reversal), parent-ed 0.158→0.069 (**57% attenuation**).
- Wealth 1985 (post-outcome; directional caveat): Black −0.431→−0.151 (**65% attenuation**), Hispanic +0.158→+0.558 (amplified positive).
- Logistic, college completion (grade>12, events 1,182/1,086): Black −0.573 (OR .56) → +0.081 (ns); Hispanic −0.513 (OR .60) → +0.526 (OR 1.69, p<1e-7); income −0.052→−0.220. Same qualitative pattern as OLS.
- **Class-rank secondary spec (B2, n=4,174) — material difference, flagged per your note:** Black attenuates a further 35% (−0.287→−0.185, p=0.04), but the Hispanic coefficient flips *back to negative* (−0.187, p=0.024) and income becomes more negative (−0.269). The ASVAB coefficient halves (0.779→0.350) due to shared variance with class rank. So the "Hispanic reversal" is robust to SES/sex choices but not to adding class rank, and B2's sample is more White (63.2%) — treat the Hispanic sign as specification-sensitive; the Black-gap attenuation is the robust, consistent finding.

**Descriptive BA (grade≥16 in 1979; n=39 total, too rare to model):** Black 0.30% (6/2,002), Hispanic 0.13% (4/3,174), White 0.39% (29/7,510). By 1979-income quintile (n≈2,000 each): Q1 0.39%, Q2 0.29%, Q3 0.24%, Q4 0.10%, Q5 0.44% — no monotonic gradient at these tiny counts (8/6/5/2/9 BAs).

**Diagnostics:** correlations (complete cases): grade–ASVAB r=0.324; grade–Black r=−0.115; grade–Hispanic r=−0.055; grade–income r=0.015; income–ASVAB r=0.241; income–Hispanic r=−0.147 — confirming the income suppression mechanism. ASVAB raw scale: +100 pts (1 SD) on the 4-section composite ≈ +0.86 grade-years.

**Limitations:** (1) No degree-attainment flag exists; the outcome is 1979 grade (baseline), so "BA completion" is proxied by the top of the grade scale — only 39 respondents had already reached grade 16. (2) 1978 family income is a weak, non-positive predictor of attainment here; the positive SES gradient is clearest for parent education and 1985 wealth. (3) Complete-case attrition shrinks n by 12–67% and shifts composition modestly toward White at later waves (differential missingness by race verified: e.g., 1985 wealth missing 15.1% Black vs 23.1% White). (4) ASVAB (1981) post-dates the 1979 grade but pre-dates adult degree completion — appropriate as an ability/mediator proxy. (5) Hispanic-coefficient sign is specification-sensitive (see class-rank note above).

payload.hypothesis: Considering academic characteristics substantially attenuates the effects of race and SES on BA-level attainment: the Black attainment gap shrinks by ~65% (−0.82 to −0.29 grade-years, still significant) and the Hispanic gap is fully mediated and reverses (−0.42 to +0.24), while the parent-education SES effect is cut by ~57% (0.158 to 0.069). The ASVAB ability composite is the strongest predictor (1 SD ≈ 0.8 grade-years, β=0.35), absorbing most of the racial gap; 1978 family income, a weak standalone predictor, shows a suppression effect (negative, significant only after ability control). Residual race/SES effects after controlling academic characteristics are small relative to ability, and the Hispanic coefficient's sign is specification-sensitive (reverses again when class-rank percentile is added).
payload.workflow: Two-stage OLS on 'Highest grade completed, 1979' (continuous; BA = grade 16): Stage A = race dummies (Black, Hispanic; ref. non-Black non-Hispanic) + log1p 1979 total net family income; Stage B = Stage A + standardized 4-section ASVAB composite (1981). Sensitivities: sex-adjusted models; parent-education composite and log1p 1985 family wealth as SES; logistic regression on college completion (grade>12); Stage B2 adding class-rank percentile (1−(rank−1)/class size). Complete-case analysis with reported n and race composition per stage; descriptive BA (grade≥16) rates by race and income quintile (n=39); correlation diagnostics for the income suppression effect.
